sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Half of our team has a grandparent living with dementia, so this idea came from something we've experienced in our own families. We've heard questions like “Have you seen my pills?” or “Where are my glasses?” repeated throughout the day. We wanted to build something that could help with those moments, both for the person looking for their things and for the family members helping them. More than 7 million Americans live with Alzheimer's disease, and most still live at home. Misplacing everyday items can be frustrating and make it harder to feel independent. Sometimes, a person may believe someone has taken their belongings. That made us interested in using photos, so there would be something concrete to refer to when helping them look. Existing tools don't fit this problem: Tracker tags only work on things you remembered to tag. Smart glasses ask someone with memory loss to remember to wear, charge, and keep track of a device, so the glasses become one more lost item. That led us to Keepsake: a camera-based memory assistant that remembers where everyday items were last seen and saves a photo. We chose a problem we knew from our own families and built something we hoped could make that part of their day a little easier.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Keepsake is a camera-based memory assistant that helps people living with dementia keep track of everyday belongings. Using a phone camera, it detects items like glasses, keys, and wallets, remembers when they were last seen, and saves a photo. Users can ask where something is and receive a spoken answer alongside the photo, with the item highlighted. The idea is to give them something they can recognize and use to retrace their steps. In a fixed room setup, Keepsake can scan furniture and use familiar locations like “near the couch” to describe where an item was seen. The phone can also be worn on a chest mount to capture items as the person moves around. In that mode, it refers to the last sighting and photo rather than treating the camera’s position as a location in the room. Of course, a camera can't see everything. An item might be covered, taken out of view, or moved after the last photo. Keepsake reports what it last saw and makes that uncertainty clear. It doesn't need tags attached to belongings, and video is processed locally on the computer.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: Camera. An iPhone streams to a Mac over Continuity Camera, selected by name so the camera index can't shift between runs. OpenCV reads the frames. Detection. Ultralytics YOLO-World ( yolov8s-worldv2 ), an open-vocabulary detector we prompt with each item's name. This finds things standard detectors can't, like keys, wallets, AirPods, and glasses. It runs at 1280 px on Apple MPS at about 5 fps, with ByteTrack for tracking and a per-item confidence threshold. Room areas. Scan room runs the larger YOLO11m model over a few still frames, keeps furniture it sees reliably, merges duplicates, and numbers repeats ("Chair 1," "Chair 2"). Each item gets the most specific area it sits in, "near the …" if it's just outside one, or the left, middle, or right of the room if nothing fits. Wearable mode. MediaPipe hand landmarks plus OpenAI CLIP embeddings. When a hand touches an item for half a second and lets go, the item is tracked. A per-item tracker follows it as held , put down , out of view , or with you , and saves the sharpest recent frame as the last-seen photo. Voice. Browser speech recognition for input; answers spoken in a user-selectable Grok voice (xAI text-to-speech), with the browser voice as a fallback. The xAI key stays on the server. App. FastAPI and SQLite on the backend; React, Vite, and Tailwind on the frontend, with a List view, a Map view drawn over the scanned room, item detail with photo history, and a privacy panel. Deterministic core. Where an item comes only from

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Our biggest challenge was switching from a stationary camera to a wearable one. We initially designed Keepsake to watch a single room, but realized that once someone left that room, it could no longer help track their belongings. Installing cameras in every room would also make the setup expensive and inconvenient. Using a phone on a wearable mount made it more accessible and allowed it to follow the person throughout their day. That decision meant rethinking much of the design. With a stationary camera, we could use furniture and fixed areas to describe where an item was. With a wearable camera, the view changes constantly, and an object disappearing from the frame might just mean the person turned around. We had to change how we tracked items, recorded memories, and decided when to give reminders, using hand interactions and the last recorded sighting instead of relying on a stable view of the room. Moving the camera introduced another problem: everything appeared to move at once. For a fixed camera, we added a scan process that rechecks the room. Wearable mode needed a different approach, using sightings and hand interactions rather than fixed room locations.

sections.heading: Accomplishments That We're Proud Of
sections.text: It doesn't lie. Moved mid-carry, camera bumped, never seen: each case gets a truthful answer instead of a confident guess. For a user who can't check the answer, that matters more than anything else. The photo is the answer. A photo of the item in the user's own room, taken the moment it was put down, ends the search and ends the argument about whether someone took it. Nothing to wear, tag, or charge. One phone on a shelf covers a whole room. Wearable mode is there when the person wants it, never required. Everything stays home. Detection, tracking, and memory all run on one laptop. Photos stay on disk under the user's control, with a switch to pause photo saving and a button to forget everything. Twelve items, zero training, thanks to open-vocabulary detection and per-item tuning.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Making plans with friends should be easy. Instead, it often turns into a long group-chat loop: “Are you free this weekend?” “Maybe.” “Where should we go?” “I don’t know.” “Someone pick something.” The plan usually dies before anyone decides on a time, place, ride, reservation, or food. Ingenium changes that by letting personal agents coordinate for people. Instead of waiting for every friend to reply, Ing can communicate with each person’s Ing to find when they are free. The group gets a real time to meet, then the right agents help turn that time into an actual plan. All designed around the app people already use to make plans: iMessage

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ingenium turns a group idea into a scheduled plan. Text Ing something like: “Find a time for dinner this week,” “Plan Maya’s birthday,” or “What should we do Saturday?” Ing can Ask your friends’ Ings when they are free. Each person’s personal agent responds with availability, so the group does not need to wait for every person to manually check and reply. Find the best shared time. Ing compares everyone’s availability and proposes a time the group can confirm. Create the event. Once a timeslot is found, each person's Ing adds the event to their calendar Call in specialists to make the plan real. Find food options. A DoorDash specialist can return delivery options, estimated delivery times, group pricing, and direct links. Plan rides. An Uber specialist can compare ride types, estimate costs, and create a link with the destination ready. Find venues, reservations, tickets, flights, gifts, or supplies. Each specialist returns a few relevant options with the details needed to decide. Build the final itinerary. After the group picks its options, Ing summarizes the plan: what is happening, when it is happening, where to go, and what each person needs to do. Research anything that needs a browser. Users can ask Ing to compare restaurants, research events, or look up options. Ing works in its own cloud browser and sends screenshots and results back through iMessage.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: iMessage coordinator with Photon: We built Ing as the main agent users text. It understands the request, decides what help is needed, starts the group chat, and combines agent responses into one final plan. Specialist-agent system: Ing can call in specialist agents for food delivery, rides, venues, restaurant reservations, tickets, shopping, flights, and itinerary planning. Each agent has a focused job and only responds when it is relevant to the conversation. Real-time group coordination: Ing waits for the agents it called in to respond, then turns their results into a clear group plan instead of leaving users with scattered recommendations. Calendar scheduling: We connected Google Calendar so Ingenium can check free/busy availability, find shared time slots in 30-minute intervals, and create an event after the group confirms. Cloud computer: We gave Ing a sandboxed browser through E2B Desktop and OpenAI computer use. When a task needs deeper research, Ing can browse, compare options, send screenshots while it works, and return a short answer with links. Privacy boundaries: All data from group chats are encrypted and only used by Ing. Calendar details are not shared with the group. Personal connected tools are only available in a user’s private conversation with Ing. Web experience: We built Ingenium’s landing page with Next.js and Tailwind CSS.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: A group chat with multiple AI agents can quickly become overwhelming if every agent replies to every message. We addressed that by giving each specialist a narrow role and a strict reply rule: agents only answer when they are directly relevant, named, or responding to their own earlier message. Otherwise, they return PASS and stay quiet. Ensuring user's data is safe, making sure what is sent in messages is encrypted and only used by Ing How do we learn an individual's boundaries and preferences. ie. are they vegetarian? do they want to go out at 8am on a Monday just because their calendar is open?

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Built a working iMessage flow where a user texts one coordinator and that coordinator can add other agents to the group chat Made specialist agents behave like focused collaborators rather than a pile of generic chatbots. Created dynamic roles for food delivery, rides, venues, reservations, tickets, shopping, flights, and planning. Built calendar availability matching that finds shared free time without revealing private event details. Added event creation and invitation sending after the group confirms a plan.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: the hard part of multi-agent systems is not only getting agents to produce answers. It is deciding who should answer, when they should stay quiet, and how to turn several partial answers into one decision a group can act on. trust matters more than having an agent do everything. Users should be able to see where recommendations came from, inspect links themselves, and keep the final decision for anything involving money, reservations, or personal information. we learned that “social good” does not always need to look like a massive platform. Helping people overcome the small coordination barriers that keep them from seeing friends can be meaningful on its own.

sections.heading: What's next for Ingineer
sections.text: Improve the planner so it can account for travel time, group size, dietary needs, budgets, and event timing in one final itinerary. Test Ingenium with real friend groups to measure whether it actually reduces back-and-forth and leads to more completed plans. Move from prototype-scale agent seats to a more reliable production architecture that does not depend on teammates’ laptops staying online.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Our inspiration was two-fold. Our project has 2 core applications: helping people find quiet spaces to hang out with their quiet friends, and in other cases helping people, from gamers to party people, avoid noise complaints and upset neighbors :) We also want something portable, accessible, and customizable, unlike the expensive decibel trackers often found in machine rooms and workshops.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our hardware can be modelled to fit both use cases. We have a responsive color gradient LED system that blinks when noise levels are below the user-specified loudness threshold. Further, our dashboard shows analytics for the quieter spots near you based on the noise recorded there over a period of time.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We used an ESP32 board as the main component to create a clean circuit and make our vision of a color gradient noise detector come to life. We used fast api to create an efficient framework and integrate the HTML code for our website. We incorporated static charts into our project using Plotly, Matplotlib, and Pandas. And lots of tinkering and troubleshooting led us to creating an MVP that works!

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Learning on a time crunch proved to be harder than we had anticipated. Handling errors and roadblocks, like smoothing out regular disturbances from our microphone input, was rougher (pun intended) than it turned out to be while we were running low on sleep. Waking up with a fresh mind and getting technical (+ moral) support from the folks at the hardware table and the CICS makerspace was motivating.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Creating a fully functioning circuit-related project with the potential for helping people. And getting to present a functioning project with a website and a tangible hardware component!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Creating a website with interactive elements was lots of fun. Tinkering with circuits to get them to work in niche ways was also incredibly satisfying. Working with microcontrollers and associated devices felt like learning how to do magic.

sections.heading: What's next for Amby
sections.text: Deploying our microcontrollers in many locations to have them send data via WiFi for displaying metrics dynamically on our website. Collecting user feedback and incorporating that to improve our product.

devpost_page.title: SlothMotion
devpost_page.tagline: SlothMotion helps the elderly stay active with personalized exercise routines, tracking movements in real time and giving instant feedback tailored to their physical condition.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: 57% of Australians aged 65 and over do not meet the recommended physical activity guidelines. Physical inactivity significantly increases the risk of chronic disease, premature mortality, and disability. It is also linked to reduced bone strength, respiratory dysfunction, and a higher likelihood of cardiovascular disease and stroke. Despite these risks, many older adults face barriers to staying active. Mobility limitations, medical conditions, lack of access to exercise facilities, and discomfort in traditional gym environments can make regular exercise difficult. We were inspired to create a solution that makes physical activity more accessible, safe, and enjoyable for older Australians. Our goal is to empower people aged 65 and over to stay active by providing guided exercises they can perform from the comfort of their own home, while taking into account their individual physical limitations.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our web app encourages older adults to stay physically active by allowing them to follow a guided exercise routine of a difficulty level of their choice personalized to their physical ailments. Our app tracks the user’s body movements and joint positions through their webcam, compares these movements with a reference routine and provides real-time feedback to help users perform exercises correctly and safely. Our interface uses high-contrast colours, large readable fonts, and clear instructions.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The frontend of our web app was developed using React with Vite, allowing us to build a responsive and simple interface tailored to older users. To detect and track body movements, we used MediaPipe Pose. MediaPipe Pose provides real-time pose estimation through the user’s webcam and extracts key body landmarks such as shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees. We implemented a pose comparison system that normalizes the user’s detected pose and compares it with a reference pose from a recorded exercise routine. By analysing differences between joint positions, the system can determine whether the movement is being performed correctly and provide immediate feedback to the user. The interface was designed with accessibility as a priority. We focused on large typography, clear navigation, and high-contrast visuals to ensure that older adults can comfortably interact with the app.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Integrating MediaPipe Pose for real-time movement tracking was a challenge. None of our team members had prior experience with computer vision, so understanding how pose detection works and how to interpret the landmark data required a significant learning curve. We needed to learn how MediaPipe represents the human body using keypoints and how to process these coordinates in a meaningful way. Another challenge was developing a reliable method to compare the user’s live movements with a reference exercise routine. We had to experiment with normalizing pose data and defining thresholds that could detect incorrect movements without being overly strict. Designing the interface for an older audience also presented unique challenges. We had to simplify our layout, increase readability, and ensure that instructions were clear and easy to follow.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Integrating MediaPipe pose detection and successfully using it to track a user’s body movements through their webcam was a major milestone for our team, especially given our lack of prior experience with computer vision. Another accomplishment was developing a system that compares a user’s movements with a reference exercise routine to provide immediate feedback. Our app allows users to understand whether they are performing exercises correctly in real time, helping them stay active while reducing the risk of injury. We were able to build an accessibility-focused interface. By prioritising high-contrast visuals, large readable fonts, and simple navigation, we've built an app that is approachable for older users who may be less familiar with technology. Overall, we are proud that we were able to turn an idea aimed at improving the health and independence of older Australians into a functional prototype within the limited time of a hackathon.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned a lot about working with computer vision and real-time pose detection. Since none of us had prior experience with MediaPipe or pose estimation, we had to quickly understand how body landmarks are detected and how those coordinates can be used to interpret human movement. We also learned the importance of designing accessible technology. Building an application for older adults required us to rethink typical interface design and focus on simplicity, readability, and clarity. This helped us better understand how thoughtful design choices can make technology more inclusive. Finally, we learned the value of rapid prototyping and teamwork under time pressure. Collaborating across frontend and backend development, computer vision, and UI design allowed us to turn our initial idea into a working prototype within the limited timeframe of the hackathon.

sections.heading: What's next for SlothMotion
sections.text: We plan to expand SlothMotion to better support a wider range of physical restrictions and medical conditions, allowing more users to safely participate in exercise routines tailored to their needs. We also aim to improve accessibility by integrating voice controls, enabling users to navigate the app and start routines without needing to interact heavily with the interface. Another feature we could implement in a future iteration is an AI assistant that can guide users through the app and answer questions. We also plan to introduce daily reminders and notifications to encourage users to maintain consistent exercise habits.

devpost_page.title: baymax
devpost_page.tagline: Baymax is a network of hospital AI agents that supports abrupt crises using weather, disease, and inventory data, then coordinates hospital-to-hospital supply transfers before crises peak.

sections.text: Baymax When a heatwave strikes, a disease outbreak surges, or a mass casualty event unfolds, hospitals are suddenly competing for the same scarce supplies, and the phone-call coordination that's supposed to fix it is far too slow. Baymax is a network of hospital AI agents built on Fetch.ai that sees crises coming by fusing live weather, disease, and inventory signals. Using Claude for reasoning, it autonomously negotiates and settles inter-facility transfers on-chain before shortages peak. Every decision is traced through Arize Phoenix, allowing the system to learn from each event and improve future responses. Baymax doesn't just respond to emergencies - it learns to anticipate them.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text: Baymax predicts shortages before they happen, negotiates inventory transfers between hospitals, settles them on-chain, and learns from every crisis it handles.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The supply crisis starts long before a hospital runs out. It starts hours earlier, when a weather forecast converges with rising illness signals and a facility that's already running lean. By the time a supply manager notices the pattern—let alone makes phone calls to neighboring facilities, negotiates terms, and arranges a transfer—the shortage has already peaked. The perception problem (counting what's on a shelf) is largely solved. The harder problem is autonomous coordination under surge conditions : seeing a crisis before it happens, negotiating transfers across institutions under real constraints, settling them quickly, and improving the system after every event. That's a multi-agent systems problem. Fetch.ai provides the agent network. Claude provides the reasoning layer. Arize Phoenix closes the learning loop. Baymax is what happens when all three work together.

sections.heading: What it Does
sections.text: Baymax runs one agent per hospital. Each agent continuously combines: Live inventory from edge vision systems Weather forecasts and disease-burden signals Historical surge patterns and outcomes When a shortage is predicted: Claude detects a surge risk before inventory reaches critical levels. The requesting hospital broadcasts a transfer request through the Fetch.ai agent network. Nearby hospitals respond with constrained offers. Claude evaluates quantity, urgency, ETA, distance, and expiry dates. If no single offer satisfies demand, Baymax automatically creates a split transfer plan. The transfer is settled through the Fetch Payment Protocol on Dorado testnet. Arize Phoenix traces the entire decision process and outcome. The result is a system that can identify shortages earlier, coordinate faster, and continuously improve over time.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: Baymax has two user-facing surfaces: ASI:One for natural-language interaction and approvals A live Flask dashboard for real-time monitoring and visualization Both are powered by the same Fetch.ai agent network and synchronized through Redis. Core Stack Component Technology Agent Network Fetch.ai uAgents Agent Discovery & Chat Agentverse + ASI:One Settlement Fetch Payment Protocol Reasoning Claude Haiku + Claude Sonnet Vision Claude Vision State Management Redis Stack Forecasting Signals Open-Meteo + disease.sh Observability Arize Phoenix Dashboard Flask Agent Network Agent Role baymax_front Requester, ASI:One interface, settlement coordinator baymax_hospital_b Surplus inventory provider baymax_hospital_c Secondary surplus inventory provider Negotiation Flow Signal Detection ↓ Shortfall Predicted ↓ Request Broadcast ↓ Offer Collection ↓ Offer Ranking ↓ Transfer Planning ↓ On-Chain Settlement ↓ Outcome Logging

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: ASI:One Echo Loops ASI:One occasionally interpreted our own agent narration as new user intent. We built filtering, cooldowns, and heuristics to prevent agents from responding to themselves. Payment Card Rendering The Fetch payment card depended on very specific metadata fields. Missing metadata caused silent failures with no visible error messages. Python 3.14 Event Loop Changes uAgents still relied on behavior removed in Python 3.14. We had to carefully manage initialization order to ensure a valid event loop existed before agent creation. Long-Running On-Chain Verification Transaction verification could stall agent execution for up to 20 seconds. We moved verification into background threads using asyncio.to_thread() .

sections.heading: Accomplishments We're Proud Of
sections.text: Live End-to-End Settlement We successfully demonstrated: Natural-language intent → surge prediction → multi-hospital negotiation → on-chain payment → confirmed transfer Real Predictive Signals Baymax combines: Live weather data Real illness data Current inventory levels to generate structured shortage forecasts before a shortage is declared. Constraint-Aware Negotiation Baymax doesn't simply match one requester to one provider. It can automatically compose split transfers when multiple facilities are required to satisfy demand. Full Decision Traceability Every prediction, ranking decision, transfer proposal, and outcome is captured in Arize Phoenix. Parallel Development The forecasting, vision, dashboard, observability, and agent teams all built independently against a shared Redis schema and integrated successfully.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: The defensible technology isn't the camera. The real value comes from creating a network that can detect, negotiate, and settle across institutional boundaries before a crisis peaks . We also learned that observability is essential for autonomous systems. The ability to trace every decision made by the system transforms Baymax from a coordination tool into a platform that can improve with experience. Finally, we learned that fail-closed design makes live demos possible. Every major dependency has deterministic fallbacks, allowing the system to remain reliable even when external services are unavailable.

devpost_page.title: TinkerFlow
devpost_page.tagline: We built TinkerFlow, an AI powered web application to help engineers, from beginners to seasoned hackers, to create projects from the resources that they have available.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We, as passionate tinkerers, understand the struggles that come with making a project come to life (especially for begineers). 80% of U.S. workers agree that learning new skills is important, but only 56% are actually learning something new . From not knowing how electrical components should be wired, to not knowing what a particular component does, and what is the correct procedure to effectively assemble a creation, TinkerFlow is here to help you ease this process, all in one interface.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: -> Image identification/classification or text input of available electronic components -> Powered by Cohere and Groq LLM, generates wiring scheme and detailed instructions (with personality!) to complete an interesting project that is possible with electronics available -> Using React Flow, we developed our own library (as other existing softwares were depreciated) that generates electrical schematics to make the fine, precise and potentially tedious work of wiring projects easier. -> Display generated text of instructions to complete project

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We allowed the user to upload a photo, have it get sent to the backend (handled by Flask), used Python and Google Vision AI to do image classification and identify with 80% accuracy the component. To provide our users with a high quality and creative response, we used a central LLM to find projects that could be created based on inputted components, and from there generate instructions, schematics, and codes for the user to use to create their project. For this central LLM, we offer two options: Cohere and Groq. Our default model is the Cohere LLM, which using its integrated RAG and preamble capability offers superior accuracy and a custom personality for our responses, providing more fun and engagement for the user. Our second option Groq though providing a lesser quality of a response, provides fast process times, a short coming of Cohere. Both of these LLM's are based on large meticulously defined prompts (characterizing from the output structure to the method of listing wires), which produce the results that are necessary in generating the final results seen by the user. In order to provide the user with different forms of information, we decide to present electrical schematics on the webpage. However during the development due to many circumstances, our group had to use simple JavaScript libraries to create its functionality.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: LLM misbehaving: The biggest challenge in the incorporation of the Cohere LLM was the ability to generate consistent results through the prompts used to generate the results needed for all of the information provided about the project proposed. The solution to this was to include a very specifically defined prompts with examples to reduce the amount of errors generated by the LLM. Not able to find a predefined electrical schematics library to use to generate electrical schematics diagrams, there we had start from scratch and create our own schematic drawer based on basic js library.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Create electrical schematics using basic js library. Create consistent outputting LLM's for multiple fields.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Ability to overcome troubles - consistently innovating for solutions, even if there may not have been an easy route (ex. existing library) to use - our schematic diagrams were custom made!

devpost_page.title: Air Command
devpost_page.tagline: A Bluetooth-enabled smart input device that listens, learns, and types for you.

sections.heading: How we built itnspiration
sections.text: This project was inspired by the need to create more accessible computing interfaces for people with limited mobility. We were motivated by the idea that simple actions like sipping and puffing through a sensor could unlock full control of a computer. The thought that we could turn basic breath patterns into mouse movements, clicks, or even keyboard shortcuts was both exciting and meaningful — technology for empowerment.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: Through this hackathon, we learned how hardware and software integration can come together to form a seamless user experience. On the hardware side, we explored differential air pressure sensors, ADC scaling, and noise filtering. On the software side, we dove into: 1. Writing HID over GATT (Bluetooth Low Energy) services in Python and C. 2, Mapping HID keycodes into byte arrays like [0x01,0,0x06,0,0,0,0,0,0] where the first byte encodes modifiers like Ctrl, and the third byte represents a letter key. 1. Using state machines to classify short sip, long puff, and continuous actions. 2. Configuring Linux device nodes like /dev/uinput and BlueZ to emulate a real keyboard and mouse.

sections.heading: How We Built It 🛠️
sections.text: 1. Hardware Layer: We connected an MPXV7002DP air pressure sensor to the BeagleBone’s ZenHat ADC, scaling the 5 V signal down safely with a resistor divider. 2. Signal Processing: Raw ADC values were converted into pressure in kPa, filtered, and classified into sip/puff gestures with timing thresholds. 3. Bluetooth HID: We attached an Asus USB-BT500 dongle, set up BlueZ with HID over GATT, and created a composite device that appears to any computer as a standard keyboard and mouse. 4. Voice & AI Extension: We added optional voice recognition and Snowflake Cortex LLM integration to map natural-language commands (like “open Chrome”) into HID key sequences.

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced ⚡
sections.text: • Electrical safety: Scaling down 5 V sensor outputs to the ADC’s 3.3 V limit without losing resolution. • BLE HID quirks: Ensuring that our HID Report Map matched the exact number of bytes in our notifications — otherwise the computer ignored our input. • Latency: Avoiding backlogged BLE notifications that caused delayed cursor movement. • Command mapping: Building a flexible system that can handle typos (like “cpoy” → copy) and still generate the correct HID array.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Hallucinations, AI jargon, non-replicable codebases: the current artificial intelligence research landscape is a rapidly expanding field with superficiality seeping into every corner of its domain. As model research steers more accessible, both the direction and execution of AI research need to be carefully vetted and tested to ensure misinformation does not become widespread in higher academia. In this light, a few questions arose: is it possible to automate the peer-review process of traditional research with LLM orchestration, how preventable are hallucinations in this context, and how far could we really break the boundaries of sustainable, verifiable academia today?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: It uses MiniBatchKMeans (clustering algorithm) on precomputed vector embeddings (numerical text representations) to generate paper clusters, an LLM (AI text model) to create cluster titles, and UMAP (dimensionality reduction) to flatten the embeddings to a 2D visualization space, where the coordinates of any given paper represent its natural-language meaning. Void Discovery: Identifies research gaps by computing a Voronoi diagram (space partitioning) and an alpha shape (boundary detection) to find maximal empty circles (voids): regions in the scatterplot with low research density. The top voids are selected, and an LLM is used to name the missing region. Paper Selection: Border papers surrounding each void are enriched with credibility-based metadata (mainly from OpenAlex) and scored using citation + recency. Eight diverse papers per void are selected using angular bucketing (diversity) and score-based filling (quality), with the top 8 moving to the next stage. Cross Pollination Model Synthesis: This is an iterative cycle where a research problem is given to an orchestration agent (central controller): the Queen Bee. Individual paper agents (Worker Bees) provide proposals (idea, rationale, predicted effect, code changes). Worker Bees are paired to generate hybrid ideas. A planning agent creates a code plan, a coding agent implements it, and a judge agent tests results, feeding them back to the orchestration agent until target accuracy is reached, producing our new model, our

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: For our agent research swarm, we used Python with Pytorch for local model development. For LLM inference, we used OpenRouter’s Nemotron 3 Super and our ASUS GX10 AI Supercomputer with Gemma4:Latest. We used SQL and FastMCP to create MCP for our research agents. For our website and frontend, we used Typescript with React and WebGL.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our largest challenge was LLM inference speed. Because we had to make the service responsive and interactive for users, we could not run very large LLMs with high reasoning levels. We started off using Nemotron 3 Super because it was cloud hosted by OpenRouter and a very powerful coding model. We also tried inclusionAI’s Ling-2.6-1T before obtaining an ASUS GX10 where we could comfortably run Gemma4:Latest with just a few seconds of delay.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of assembling such a complex and well-organized agentic AI workflow for research. We had to manage the communication, memory, and context between over 6 agents across the entire research iteration process. This meant building a robust MCP for our agents to categorize and store information in. We also had several levels of agentic management using orchestration and feedback agents that would organize and direct the research of the sub-agents.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned about the entire LLM agent orchestration process. Reliable research and development with AI agents is not as simple as just typing a prompt into one agent! To fully utilize the power of agentic development, we learned to manage and oversee agents as a large research team, with each agent being assigned a specialization and focus. This was our first time working with MCP at this scale and also doing inference at this scale and speed.

sections.heading: What's next for beehyv
sections.text: Using more compute, we hope to increase the quantity of research output. We will be able to run larger state-of-the-art models that can produce more modern and accurate code.

sections.heading: The challenge and who it's for
sections.text: The people we love most are the ones we call least. Not because we don't care — because starting a call is friction: is she busy? is it a bad time? what do I even say? So we default to a "miss you" text, and months go by. Nudge is for anyone with someone they keep meaning to call — a parent in another city, a sibling, a college friend, a grandparent. Specifically the pairs who want to talk more but keep bouncing off the "is now okay?" problem. There are no roles and no group features: one friendship, two phones.

sections.heading: How it strengthens human connection (meaningfully, not metrically)
sections.text: Nudge removes the three things that stop a call from happening, and it does it without turning friendship into a streak or a notification farm: It finds the moment. Both phones share only free/busy blocks from their calendars (never event titles) plus on-device signals — Focus mode, driving, whether the phone is awake. When both of you are free right now , both phones get one nudge. A nudge is a mutual invitation: either person can Skip with a reason, and the other side just sees "Not right now." It makes the call better. During the video call, when you say "remember the hike last weekend?" the photo appears in your own mini window with an Ask first card. Tap Show and it's on Mom's screen. Conversations stop being "how are you… fine" and become show-and-tell. It carries the thread. Afterwards Nudge writes a short summary you both can see and delete. Topics with follow-ups ("physics exam Thursday") seed the next nudge: "Want to ask Mom how the exam went?" Every one of those steps is opt-in and symmetric — nothing happens to the other person without their acceptance. That's the point: the app is a good friend who says "you're both free, want me to connect you?", not a machine that guilt-trips you.

sections.heading: Why AI is essential (and where it isn't)
sections.text: Nudge's core feature — photos that appear because you mentioned them — is impossible without AI, and we built it entirely on Amazon Bedrock first-party models: Amazon Nova Lite reads the live transcript one line at a time and decides is this a reference to a photo, and what would you search for? ("the hike last weekend" → hike mountains last weekend ). It also captions every indexed photo, writes the post-call summary, extracts follow-up topics, and drafts the "in a meeting until 4" auto-replies. Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 puts your photos and the spoken query into the same 1,024-d vector space. Photos are embedded image-only (our eval showed it beat caption fusion: top-1 1.00 vs 0.95). Amazon S3 Vectors stores those embeddings and answers each query scoped to the speaker's own photos only . Amazon Rekognition + Nova gate what ever gets indexed: moderation labels, OCR for documents/IDs/screenshots, and a Nova "is this sensitive?" pass. 9/9 sensitive fixtures were excluded; 0/7 benign ones wrongly excluded. We measured it rather than hoped: the detector scores precision 1.000 / recall 0.896 on a 140-window eval set with 0/30 hard-negative false positives , retrieval is top-1 1.000 on a 60-photo CC0 set, and end-to-end transcript → suggestion runs at ~1.0 s p50 against the deployed stack. sections.heading: Why it's original
sections.text: Most "stay in touch" apps take one of two shapes: reminder lists / streak counters, or scheduling — put a call on the calendar for Thursday at 7. Scheduling sounds responsible, but it is a high-commitment act: you are promising your future self and someone else's future self, and people quietly resent and abandon those promises (the event gets moved, then skipped, then the app gets deleted). Nudge is deliberately low-friction and low-commitment : nothing is ever scheduled. It waits until you are both free right now, asks each of you with a single tap, and if either says "not now" nothing happened and nobody was let down. Because saying yes costs nothing and saying no costs nothing, people keep using it — the app never becomes a chore you owe someone. Beyond that, Nudge is different in four concrete ways: Mutual availability, not reminders. Both calendars have to be free; both people have to accept. Nobody is ever "reminded" to bother someone who is busy. The camera roll joins the conversation. We haven't seen another calling app that listens for "remember when…" and surfaces the actual photo — privately to the speaker first, then shared with one tap. Ask first, always. Nothing leaves your phone by voice alone. The suggestion appears in your window; the friend sees nothing until you tap Show. sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Before a clinical trial can enroll a single patient at a hospital, the sponsor and that hospital have to agree on a clinical trial agreement. A sponsor sends the same form contract to dozens of sites, and each one sends it back with its own redline. Contract staff then review every tracked change by hand, including the many that the sponsor's own negotiation playbook already answers. Across 61 cancer centers, study start-up took a median of 167 days against a 90-day target , and slow site activation is linked to missed enrollment goals ( Contemp Clin Trials Commun , 2025). We wanted to understand what that delay actually costs, so we priced it. Each week a site's contract stays open pushes the whole trial back by that site's share of enrollment, and a day of trial time is worth the chance the drug is approved times its daily sales (discounted back to today), plus the direct cost of running the trial: $$ \text{Cost of delay per week} = 7 \cdot w \cdot \left( \frac{p \cdot S}{(1+r)^{T}} + C \right) $$ where $w$ is the site's share of the study's enrollment rate, $p = 9.3\%$ is the Phase II solid-tumor chance of approval, $S = \$840{,}000$ is median oncology sales per day, $r = 10.5\%$ is the discount rate, $T = 7.6$ years to launch, and $C = \$23{,}737$ is Phase II trial cost per day (Tufts CSDD 2024; BIO/Informa/QLS 2021; DiMasi 2016). sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Siteline turns a sponsor's past negotiating positions into a central playbook and applies it to every redline that comes in. A contract manager uploads a site's Word redline, or the site simply emails it in, and within seconds every tracked change is sorted into one of four outcomes: Accept , Fallback (send the playbook's counter-language), Escalate to an approver, or Human review . Each decision shows the rule that fired, the values pulled from the clause, and a verbatim quote from the contract that Siteline has checked against the document. The review screen is the contract itself, shown in full, with every redline tinted by its outcome so a change is always judged alongside the clauses around it. Escalations go to the right person's phone. Legal, finance and privacy approvers each get an iMessage and reply 1 (approve), 2 (counter) or 3 (reject), and the decision updates live on the review screen. If they don't answer, Siteline calls them. When every change is settled, Siteline exports the counter-proposal as a Word file with real tracked changes and comments, ready to send back to the site. Across the portfolio, a ranked view shows which sites are blocking activation, how many clauses are stuck, and how much money each one is costing per week.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The core design rule is that the AI never makes the decision. It reads the contract and reports facts, and deterministic code decides what happens next. Parsing in isolation (Daytona): each uploaded .docx is parsed inside a fresh Daytona sandbox with networking turned off. Only JSON comes back out, and the sandbox is deleted afterwards. The app shows each step with its measured time, so a sponsor can see the contract never touched the open internet. Extraction: an LLM (GPT-5, with a Claude Code fallback through claude -p ) reads each change and fills a strict JSON schema with clause values. Every value has to come with a verbatim quote, and we check that quote against the document text. Rules engine: a 9-clause, 37-position playbook that we wrote the way a sponsor's contracts team would, with standards, counters, escalation triggers and talking points. The numbers in the playbook are exactly what the engine reads, and every decision carries a rule ID. Anything uncertain (a quote that fails verification, confidence below 0.80, a term no rule covers, an error) goes to a person and is never accepted automatically. Approvals (Photon 2.0 + voice): one iMessage per escalation, with a phone-call fallback. Precedents (Supabase Postgres + S3): terms from agreements that people have confirmed become precedents for future negotiations. Siteline never learns from its own automated decisions. sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our first full eval scored 79.0% , and most of the failures came from small, very literal problems. Twenty-two rows failed only because the model wrapped verbatim quotes in curly quotation marks. One clause had its carve-out narrowed to "intentional fraud", the model rounded that to "gross negligence", and it was accepted, which was our only unsafe accept. We fixed that by requiring the quote for a negligence carve-out to actually contain those words. Changing only a notice period was being read as granting termination for convenience, which caused eight false escalations. Each fix made the system stricter about what counts as evidence, not more clever. We also ran into rate limits, because the full extraction prompt with the playbook is about 9,400 tokens. To keep iteration fast, we cache each model answer under a hash of its exact prompt. That brought a full re-run of the eval from over a minute down to about two seconds, while the quote checks and rules still run fresh every time. Finally, Photon 2.0 works very differently from classic Photon, so we built the approval flow directly against its new API.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Every case Siteline didn't escalate went to human review rather than being decided, so nothing was settled without a person or a rule standing behind it. In contract work that is the trade we want to make. We're also proud that every piece of the demo is real end to end: real tracked changes in a full 17-article fictional agreement, real texts to real phones, and a real Word file at the end.

sections.text: Three AI Financial Advisors : Sofia (Financial Literacy), Marcus (Investment Education), and Luna (Behavioral Coaching) Inclusive Design : Works for users with or without traditional bank accounts Real-time Notifications : Proactive financial insights via WebSocket connections Personalized Dashboard : Adapts to user profiles and financial goals Interactive Learning : Gamified financial education modules Multi-persona Support : Built-in user personas for diverse financial situations

sections.heading: 🚀 Quick Start
sections.text: Prerequisites Node.js 18+ and npm Python 3.8+ and pip Google Gemini API key Frontend Setup # Install dependencies npm install # Start development server npm run dev Backend Setup # Navigate to backend directory cd backend # Install Python dependencies pip install -r requirements.txt # Set up environment variables cp .env.example .env # Add your Google Gemini API key to .env # Start the backend server python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

sections.heading: 🏗️ Technology Stack
sections.text: Frontend React 18 with TypeScript Vite for fast development and building Tailwind CSS for responsive styling shadcn/ui for consistent UI components WebSocket for real-time communication Backend FastAPI with async/await support WebSocket connections for real-time notifications Google Gemini AI for intelligent financial advice SQLite for data persistence

sections.heading: 📱 Usage
sections.text: Complete the Onboarding Quiz : Tell us about your financial situation, goals, and background Explore Your Dashboard : View personalized metrics and insights Chat with AI Advisors : Get instant, tailored financial guidance Receive Proactive Notifications : Stay informed about important financial opportunities Learn and Grow : Use our interactive learning modules to improve financial literacy
